newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bank Julius Baer lowers Swiss GDP forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Bank Julius Baer lowers Swiss GDP forecasts.

text.p: Bank Julius Baer said in its latest economic report for Switzerland that it was lowering its forecasts for the country's gross domestic product (GDP) for both 1997 and 1998.

"Although we are still betting on an exchange-rate induced recovery in exports this year, and, more especially in 1998, the figures available for the other sectors have prompted us to reduce our forecast for GDP growth for 1997 from 0.5 percent to minus 0.1 percent, and for 1998 from 1.7 percent to 1.1 percent," the bank said.
In 1996 Swiss GDP growth was a negative 0.7 percent.
Baer said it saw no possibility of a rapid improvement in the Swiss labour market, and also did not expect consumer sentiment to improve, especially given likelihood of only small wage increases.

Any wage increases were likely to be wiped out by higher taxes. It noted that there was also a chance that the Swiss value-added tax could be raised by one percent to finance the Swiss government pension fund, AHV.

It said the outlook for construction was not much better, and the machinery industry, Switzerland's major exporter, "had the lowest order books ever recorded since the relevant statistics have existed" at the end of 1996.
Given substantial government deficits, "the leeway for fiscal policy to stimulate the economy seems extremely limited," Julius Baer said.
It saw the main hopes for the Swiss economy tied to the weaker Swiss franc's stimulus on exports, and hopes for improvements in the European economy.

It also noted the Swiss National Bank had remained tolerant of an increase in its money supply. It was expected to keep a rise in Swiss capital market yields in bounds so as to offset any influx in international investment capital ahead of the start of the joint European currency set for January 1, 1999.
